utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is open. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the Office of the Prosecutor. Good morning to the Defence. Good morning to the witness and to all the staff members assisting the Court. The Court is going to sit in compliance with Article 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, so we're going to proceed with the cross-examination which was started yesterday by Ms. Edgerton. So, Ms. Edgerton, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak. Did you rest well overnight?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back largely today to matters that were discussed in both your testimony in chief and when we were speaking yesterday. To begin with, at pages 8043 and 8044 of your testimony yesterday, you were asked whether you were able to deal with the civilian victims of the war in the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the Bosnian army, and you said: "No, because the security services centre of Serb Sarajevo did not cover that territory." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also said: "If there had been an incident, we were often willing and ready to intervene through UNPROFOR and other international organisations that were active in the area. We were willing to extend our assistance to the other side, but the other side was never interested." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can I take from this that you're saying you actually did extend offers of assistance?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through international organisations, mainly UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall any occasions where you did that, when they took place, what they related to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was at the Markale II when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall at any other time from 1992 right through to 1995, when you made that offer?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, on the occasion of the murder of the vice prime minister of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we investigated that crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was actually in 1993, I think, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're talking about the killing of Hakija Turajlic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apart from these two occasions, can you recall any other times at which you offered your assistance to the other side in the investigation of shelling or sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other side never approached us for assistance. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection there were two occasions and only two over the course of 44 months where you offered assistance to the other side?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally, yes, but maybe there were others. I was not the only person involved in these tasks in the territory of eastern Sarajevo, the Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, then, yesterday do you recall when I asked you whether you knew about the fact that civilians in the city were falling victim to various types of gun-fire, you said you had no knowledge of that. But now based on your answer and your reference to Markale II, it sounds like you did have knowledge that there was some shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, there were victims on both sides. There were victims in the territory under the control of the VRS as well as in the territory under the control of the BH army. However, I personally, as I've already told you, I'm not familiar with the sniping victims in Sarajevo because we were not in a position to check and control whether this was happening. It is only to be assumed that there were victims on both sides. There were victims on our sides and there must have been victims on the other as well. It was wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, my question was if at the two occasions which the witness mentioned, was there ever any investigation done from your side on these two incidents. I understand that you offered your assistance to the other side, but did you do anything else than just offering your assistance? Was any steps taken -- were any steps taken to -- to actually investigate these two incidents from your side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993 we carried out an investigation independently, that was in the first case; and in the second case, we were not in a position to investigate because we did not have an insight into the investigation material and everything else that was found at Markale II. What we could see in the media and what was presented from Sarajevo drew us to conclude - and I'm speaking from the experience because I often attended sites where shells were falling and people were being killed - it was impossible that one 120-millimetre shell resulted in so many victims. In 1992 I was in a position to see a shell falling some 15 metres away from me. I was in a car with a colleague who was in the other car. Two colleagues were next to the car. One colleague died from that shelling, and those of us who were in the vehicles, we didn't even suffer a scratch. We just suffered consequences of detonation. We were listening to what UNPROFOR was saying. We wanted to go to the site of the incident but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Was any information on what had happened on the other side offered to you through UNPROFOR? In other words, did UNPROFOR provide you with information that would have enabled you to investigate those incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to me personally. I don't know whether any of the representatives of the VRS were given such information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilian police did not receive any such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to follow-up on the answer you gave to Judge Harhoff, I note that you said with respect to Markale II, what you could see in the media and what was presented from Sarajevo drew you to make some conclusions. But, sir, yesterday when I asked you about the siege of the centre of Sarajevo, you said you could only talk about what you saw with your own eyes and the investigations you participated in or in the investigations that your personnel conducted. So the assertion that you've just made about the shell that fell on Markale II is actually something that you didn't see with your own eyes and was not investigated by any of your team. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the shell falling with my own eyes, but I had an occasion to follow the media and media conveyed the image from the site on the first day, and I also have other experience, not only the experience from 1992 or 1995. I had my own police experience from 2006 and 2007 when my team got hold of some more material relative to the event in Markale. So I had an occasion to more attentively observe all the video material that was accessible to me at the time. When I was watching that video material, I could spot some illogical things. That's one thing. And second of all, we got hold of some expert analysis provided by medical forensic experts, ballistic experts, analysed the case, and based on what I perused, I have given you my opinion. So my opinion is not based only on what I knew in 1995, but also on the experience that I have gathered in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, sir, yesterday you said you found the media and media coverage unreliable when I asked you about what it portrayed about the siege. So why now today are you saying you placed some measure of faith in what the media was reporting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I trusted media. I said that I trusted the image. The camera that recorded things on the spot. I don't trust the comments, but I trust the facts, the pictures that you can see, the images that you can see if you look and watch carefully the video footage that was taken at Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, sir, that's not what you said yesterday. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, this is not what you said yesterday," said my learned friend. I believe that she should be more specific and say what she was referring to. My learned friend, with all due respect, this is not what you said yesterday. Could my learned friend be more specific and tell the witness what is it that she is specifically referring to in order to avoid confusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At page 8085, Witness, you said: "I know that the media covered the events in a very biased manner, even including the incidents I myself investigated. So, really as a professional, I could not credit the reports that were published in the media at all." Sir, would you agree with me that's what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I did say yesterday, but today I am not talking about media reports. I'm talking about the images that I had an occasion to see, and the analysis that were provided by forensic experts on medicine, ballistics, and explosives. I am not talking about what the journalists said. I'm talking about what the experts had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you -- do you have any kind of forensic expertise, sir? Are you a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed police academy, and one of my courses was crime prevention, crime tactics, crime methodology, crime operations. I completed courses for crime technician, for operative. I completed ICITAP school and I am an instructor for investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no ballistics expertise? You're not a ballistician, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that today, although I have some basic knowledge in ballistics that are applied in the crime prevention technology.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So with respect to some aspects of the siege of Sarajevo, even though you weren't there and you didn't receive reports on those incidents from any members of your team and you have no expertise, it seems as though, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a complex question. First of all, the witness has never mentioned "siege." This is happening for the third time. I did not react before. The question contains the issue of the siege. Neither in the information in chief nor in the cross did the witness mention the word "siege." The Prosecutor may follow that course, but first he has to ask the witness to provide his explanation of this notion. This is a very important word and very important for the entire case. Not for a single moment has the witness mentioned the word "siege" in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, the Defence is raising the issue of the siege of Sarajevo, which had not been covered in the examination-in-chief. Now, what have you got to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honours, I would suggest that the siege of Sarajevo is at the heart of the Prosecution's case and I'm entitled to put my case to the witness in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Court authorises you to put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, sir, with respect to some aspects of the siege of Sarajevo, even though you weren't there on site, you didn't receive reports on those incidents from any members of your team, and you have no expertise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can the witness please first be asked to explain the notion of "siege" before any other questions are asked. You are right. This question should be permitted, but let's start from the notion of "siege." Why isn't the witness asked to explain his idea of that notion, and everything else can follow from there. The -- my learned friend cannot just go straight into the word "siege" and put her questions from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I suggest you raise this issue in your re-examination if you wish to put questions to the witness about the siege. And I must also say that it would be good if we could proceed with the examination and the cross-examination and the re-examination without too many interruptions because it's better if we can get a good flow of the proceedings here. So you should put your questions about the siege to the witness when you have the chance to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, I don't intend to put any questions about the siege. In my opinion, there was no siege during the time of the indictment and it has never been my intention to put any questions to the witness about the siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now we're going to listen to the Prosecutor. She's going to put her question and the witness will answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try again slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to some aspects of the continued shelling and sniping of Bosnian-held Sarajevo over the course of 44 months, from 1992 to 1995, even though you weren't there, you didn't receive reports on those incidents from any members of your team, and you have no ballistic expertise, it seems as though you are prepared to offer opinions. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. I don't agree that during that period between 1992 and 1995, like you are trying to put it to me and you are trying to make me say it, there was no systematic shelling and sniping in Sarajevo, especially when we're talking about the period between 1994, the second half of 1994, and the beginning of the Muslim offensive in the territory that was inhabited by the Serbs, which is also part of the town of Sarajevo. It's not somewhere on the hills or in the mountains because Grbavica, Dobrinja, Hadzici, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Trnovo, all those were Sarajevo municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Mr. Tusevljak. With respect, that wasn't the answer to the question I put to you at all, but I'm going to move on. Yesterday when we were talking about whether your service ever referred allegations of war crimes against civilians perpetrated by a member of the SRK to the military Prosecutor's office and to the military investigating judge, you talked at page 8098 and 8099 about what effectively was a cooperative arrangement between your service and the SRK. For example, you stated, in addition to yourself as head of the service, there were also departments, each of which had a head that could have had cooperation with these organs of the SRK. You said any one of your associates could have handed over an investigation into an SRK war crimes perpetrator without it having to reach you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I'm testifying, I'm not only talking about war crimes, but about all crimes because there were crimes pertaining to the area of general crimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Which were most grievous and which means that a member of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about war crimes and I think I've made that clear both yesterday and today. You just indicated you recalled that, so I'd like to ask you this: In light of this cooperative relationship, were you ever asked by the SRK to provide assistance in any of their police investigations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parts of my crime technology were put at the disposal of the military prosecutors and investigating judges of the Romanija-Sarajevo Corps. I'm talking about equipment, not personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that for the investigation of allegations of war crimes against members of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall between 1992 and 1995, one single instance in which you came upon or undertook an investigation of war crimes against a member of the SRK that you had to refer to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as war crimes go, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to two of the incidents you testified about yesterday, three in fact. The first one being with respect to shelling in the Ilidza area in which two young boys were killed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps in that regard, I could ask for D299 to be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document which you talked about yesterday, if I'm not mistaken, is an official report into a shelling that occurred in Rakovica area in Ilidza around the 18th of June, 1995, and I'd like to direct you to what I think is the second page of this report in B/C/S, also the second page of the English translation. The bottom of the first paragraph of this second page which says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you speak closer to the microphone, Mr. Witness, otherwise the interpreters find it difficult to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... On the page --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: See the page on the screen in front of you, please look at the bottom of the first paragraph where it says, that this incident related to an exploding artillery shell of undetermined calibre fired by members of the so-called BH army from the direction of Godusa village, Visoko municipality. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How far is Visoko from Sarajevo and in what direction?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visoko is about 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo. However, from this location, Ilidza municipality borders on Visoko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this shell, according to reports of your service, did not originate from the centre of Sarajevo at all, did it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It came from the area of Visoko, or rather, from the area of Visoko municipality, as stated here, from the direction of village Godusa in Visoko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How was that determination made? How was it determined that the shell came from Godusa village in Visoko municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely we received that information from the SRK since their scouts who were on the lines probably knew what direction the firing came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "most likely," that's because you actually had no involvement in this investigation at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I participated personally because Dusko Obradovic is my crime investigator as well as the other men mentioned here. They were members of my team, I was their immediate superior and I sent them to the scene. I waited for them when they returned, and I was sent their report the very same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you participated personally, why isn't your name on any of the reports? Is that because you only acted in a supervisory capacity and weren't directly involved in the investigations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from being their superior, I also often took part in on-site investigations. This on-site investigation record is an essential part of the overall crime report that was submitted to the prosecutor. My signature must be underneath the conclusions of the entire file, and I repeat, this record is a part of that file.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, how was it determined that this shell was fired by members of the so-called BH army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read it again. It is clear that it could have only come from the BH side and fired by members of the BH army, not from the Serb side. This is the shell who -- which killed the two boys. It wasn't the only shell that landed that day in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why do you feel you're able to say that this shell doesn't come from the Serb side? What conclusive evidence have you got?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this was not the only shell to land in that area that day. Many more fell. I think this was on the 17th, the second or the third day into the offensive, when the artillery activity on these areas was of such intensity that basically you couldn't even peek out. That's why the on-site investigation was not conducted the first day when the event took place, but rather on the 17th -- no, the event was on the 17th, and we carried out the investigation the next day, once the shelling had stopped. As you can see, the date says that it was drafted on the 18th, whereas it mentions the event of the 17th. We waited for one whole day because of the shelling. We couldn't have conducted the investigation any sooner than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So because of the circumstances, by the time you got to the scene -- between the time of the incident and the time you got to the scene, the scene wasn't actually secured, was it, because of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely clear that there was no interference, that no one tried to move the bodies. Since even if you arrive on the scene late, one of the basic questions to be put is to ask the witness who found the bodies whether he moved anything or changed anything. This is also easily confirmed by the investigation itself to see whether bodies were moved or not. If there were, there would be blood traces on the ground and the scene would be contaminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you're saying all this without even having gone to the scene in this case, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have the report of my operatives who were on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on, please, to D300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, based on the registry's calculation, you have used an hour and a 20 minutes for this cross-examination, which was supposed to last for an hour and a half. So you have about ten minutes left. So please do try to do your best.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I suspect I will run a risk of outlasting my ten minutes probably by an additional ten minutes, with Your Honour's leave. But I will be as expeditious as I possibly can. In any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: D300 is now on the screen. Sir, you weren't involved in this investigation either, were you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the scene; however, I participated in the forwarding of the report. The on-site investigation was headed by an investigating judge, in this case Vladimir Jankovic. My operatives assisted him during the investigation, as you can see from the composition of the investigative team. All the people enumerated here, the inspectors and technicians, are my operatives, my technicians, who I sent to the scene. The event itself --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the basis of the determination in this case that the fire came from ABiH forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in addition to the official report there are photographs explaining it, and could you please show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think they were admitted as parted of this exhibit, if we could scroll through.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're unable to answer the question as to the determination of the origin of fire without referring to photographs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do it even without photographs, but it would be far easier if we could have a look at the photographs, since it's been 12 years since the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the photograph on the top of the -- in the centre of your screen?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the sports hall. The boy was hit on the stairs. Can we go on? What is shown here is the exact location where the boy had been hit and blood traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How does that --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How does that go to establish origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be the last photograph at which you will see the origin of fire or its direction. The boy was seated at the staircase. This is another image of the scene. You can go on. What you can see here is the direction from which the bullet had come.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And ...?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can be seen, this is the most likely location from which the enemy sniper fired. If you move on, you will see --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, let me ask you a question now, sir. What's the basis of the determination that the fire came from BiH forces then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I'm going to leave that and move on. Let's go, sir, to the shooting of the two girls which you talked about at page 8071 of your testimony. You seem to have some familiarity with that investigation, and I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about it. You wouldn't know, would you, sir, that the day after the incident on 12 March 1995, Bosnian authorities stated to UN officials that their government had formed a commission to investigate the incident?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You wouldn't know that shortly after --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, that evidence is found in P24.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You wouldn't know that shortly after the shooting the General Staff of the Bosnian army confirmed that a Muslim sniper was responsible and stated that the soldier who had killed the girls had been arrested and would stand trial?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since a lot of time has passed between 1995 and today, perhaps we could see the judgement issued in that case. If they knew who the person was who had killed the girls, until now the judgement must have been rendered but I know of no such case in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the source of that information, Your Honours, is P26.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You wouldn't know that General Milosevic himself was aware that the Bosnian authorities had said they were taking measures with the perpetrator of the incident, would you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. General Milosevic was in no way my superior at that time. We had no such communication. We were under no obligation to inform each other of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You wouldn't -- you asked for the record of conviction, so then I take it from that you wouldn't know that the perpetrator, one Senad Piskic, was prosecuted, convicted, and sentenced to a term of imprisonment for the event doctor for the incident?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw the document and this is the first time I hear of it and the first time that I've heard of Senad Piskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have ter number 03419 brought up on the screen, please, and I should say page -- I've seen these yesterday in e-court, so I know they exist in e-court. And page 2 of this same document, Mr. Registrar, should be the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see on the screen in front of you a letter from the acting minister of defence -- a letter from the acting minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina referring to a military card for one Senad Piskic, and noting that the person in question was prosecuted and sentenced to a year's-long imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think this document you received is incomplete. What is lacking -- well, it says based on the information available we can inform you the person was prosecuted and sentenced to year's-long imprisonment. First of all, they should have forwarded the exact file number of the case and they should have specified what was the term of imprisonment. When we forward such documents, we always specify the exact reference number, we specify the imprisonment term, and according to my knowledge, because I also deal with such issues today, I don't think he was ever sentenced and sent to jail. I know of many others graver crimes committed by members of the ABiH --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, thank you --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- And those persons were not prosecuted for war crimes but for general crimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I take it from the first part of your answer that you're disputing the veracity of the information contained in this document. You're saying that this document forwarded by the acting minister of defence is untrue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not stating that. Based on what they forwarded to you, one cannot see whether this person was indeed sent to prison and for how long. There's no reference file number. They only sent his card and the daily combat report of the command, and that's it. And my apologies, but I also wanted to say that the documentation on the -- these proceedings might exist in the archives of the military court, which means that this lady --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Had no access so it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- She only said there may be documentation. The question is whether there is any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- My question to you required a yes or no answer. Are you agreeing or disagreeing with the veracity of the document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is admitted. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object the tendering of this document and its being admitted as a Prosecution exhibit. It doesn't contain even the basic elements necessary to establish whether there was a proceedings conducted against anyone. If it contains no judgement, perhaps they could have at least mentioned the number of the file of the proceedings and the prison term imposed, and then it might be a relatively reliable document. As such, this document contains nothing that would confirm to us that this person, indeed, was held responsible, that he stood trial, and was issued with a judgement, and no one can check that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe that the test for admitting a document into evidence through a witness is not whether the information in it is correct or incorrect. The test is rather whether there is any bearable relation between the document and the witness. And I must admit that it is perhaps difficult to establish the relation between the witness and this document because he says that he has no knowledge of it and he cannot confirm or otherwise have any opinion about the contents. So I don't know. What do you say, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I tendered it because it goes to the witness's credibility, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The document has been admitted and we accept your reason.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me for the interruption, that will go in as P813.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, do not talk to us, please, about the document. The document is already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then there's nothing for me to say. I cannot understand how this has anything to do with the reliability and credibility of this witness, and it has nothing to do with him since he said that he knows nothing of this and he pointed out the lacking information. How can that go to the credibility of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber heard your comments, and we will deliberate on it. Ms. Edgerton, I believe that you have two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then I'll ask, with your permission, one more question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do you recall speaking to a reporter from the New York Times during the time of the re-integration in 1996 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honours, it will be three more brief questions related to the same topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall during the discussion with that reporter about aspects of the re-integration saying to him: "My loyalty is to the Serbian leadership in Pale. The Muslims have no interest in professional police work. They only want to create an Islamic state. They can't expect us to help them do that"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know at the time you made this statement that Radovan Karadzic, the head of the Serbian leadership in Pale, had been indicted by this Tribunal for genocide?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic is not the only representative of the Serb people, and he wasn't the only person in the Serbian leadership. When I said this, I did not want to say that he was my boss. What I had in mind was completely different. I had no Radovan Karadzic in mind when saying that. He's not the only person who can represent or speak on behalf of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you know at the time you made this statement that he had been indicted for genocide?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, but when I uttered these words I did not have Radovan Karadzic in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said you recalled saying: "The Muslims have no interest in professional police work. They only want to create an Islamic state." Do you also recall referring to those Muslims in -- as fanatics during the course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims as fanatics, well I have 40 videotapes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with three hours of material each about the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, that was a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 03407 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the document is brought up on the screen and before the witness, I have to say that my learned friend is incorrectly quoting the contents of the article. He said -- actually, the journalist wrote that Mr. Tusevljak was sitting under the large photo of Radovan Karadzic, but he himself never mentioned Radovan Karadzic. The journalist himself mentioned that the interviewee was sitting under Radovan Karadzic's photograph during the interview, whereas the interviewee himself never mentioned Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very strange. I was under the impression that the witness was saying yes to the question put by the Prosecutor, but the Prosecutor may always put the question again just to make sure that we're talking about the same thing. Would you like the witness to be asked the same question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand -- I would understand that the witness would have been able to answer if he had the document in front of him while he was answering the question. Maybe the witness can say something about this now. The journalist wrote that while he spoke to him, he was sitting under Radovan Karadzic's photo. He, himself, never mentioned Radovan Karadzic's name in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, would you be able to clarify this point with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect -- with respect, if we go back to page 22, line 19, you will see that I quoted the article almost verbatim, and when quoting the article I did not refer to Radovan Karadzic. My question at line 25 was: "Did you know at the time you made this statement that Radovan Karadzic, the head of the Serb leadership in Pale, had been indicted by this Tribunal for genocide?" With respect, Your Honours, my question was absolutely not a mis-characterization or a misquoting of the article. I -- my question was simply whether he knew that at the time he made that statement, Karadzic had been indicted for genocide. I didn't even mention that he was sitting under a picture of Karadzic at the time; my friend brought that up in evidence. If I may, Your Honours, I'd like to continue so that I can finish up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic, while Ms. Edgerton was talking we were able to check what was said, and it seems to me that what you were mentioning was not said here. The text on the transcript is different from what you are saying to us. So you may continue, please, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see the translation of this article in your language on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the first paragraph, would you agree with me, says: "Simo Tusevljak, the chief of the criminal division for the Serbian police in this suburb of Sarajevo, is required to uphold the laws and constitution of what he calls 'those Muslim fanatics' in his more diplomatic moments." Does that refresh your memory as to what you said during the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm standing by these words. Muslims are not interested in the professional police work. They only want their Islamic state and they can't expect us to help them with that. Everything above that are the journalists comments rather than my words. Also, as far as I can remember, I did not receive this journalist in my own office, so I don't know what was on the wall of that office at the time. As for what the journalist wrote, I don't know; I only know what I stated. He came to me and said that there was a plan for the time-period to be extended, the 45 [as interpreted] time-period, but as far as I know, there was never such a plan in place. Nobody ever offered us to stay on in the police on the Bosnian side. And you know only too well that over 120.000 Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were moved from that area during that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was: "Does that refresh your memory of what you said during the course of that interview?" And your answer was: "I'm standing by these words," being the following: "Muslims are not interested in professional police work, they only want their Islamic state, and they can't expect us to help them with that." Those are the words you're standing by?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've forgotten to tender this newspaper article, please, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is admitted. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P814, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please refresh my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- my memory about where was this published. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The New York Times, Your Honour, and it was recovered from the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: On the 5th of February, 1996. Thank you very much. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have a few questions, but due to the time constraints I will have to reduce their number. But since we're talking about the document that is still on the screen and in front of the witness -- or maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph of this document it is stated this, only two words under the quotation mark as having been uttered by Witness Simo Tusevljak, "Muslim fanatics," nothing else has been added and nor can one see in what context were these words uttered, if he uttered them at all. He has just started explaining what kind of documentation he has, but I would like to ask him what was the context in which these words were uttered. Do you remember, did you ever reflect on these words? Did you ever utter the words "Muslim fanatics" --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, that's an incredibly leading question, I would submit, and ask that it be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have absolutely not been leading the witness. In the first paragraph there are two words between the quotation marks, and those are "the Muslim fanatics," and I'm only asking the witness to try and remember. I'm not leading the witness. I'm only asking him to try and remember what the context was when the "Muslim fanatics" were mentioned. This is a document that was put to the witness by the Prosecution, and if the Prosecutor insisted on these two words, I suppose that the witness should be allowed to explain what he meant by these two words, because taken out of the context these two words don't mean a thing, do they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this was taken out of the context. I suppose that we must have been talking about the Mujahedin, which were actively involved in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and whose number was huge at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Witness, this concludes your testimony. On behalf of this Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to bring your contribution to international justice with your testimony. On my behalf and on behalf of all the people who were present here in this courtroom, I would like to wish you a safe trip. Thank you very much. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we still have 15 minutes, and we better make good use of them. Who is the next witness and is it a protected witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the following witness is not protected. This is T-35, Mr. Ljuban Mrkovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: T-38 is the witness's number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ljuban Mrkovic. On behalf of this Trial Chamber I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague, and I just want to make sure that you understand me in your own language. If you do, please say you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will now make a solemn declaration. The usher will give you the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. You may be seated. According to the procedure and to the practice of this Trial Chamber, I will ask the Defence counsel to identify you by asking you some usual questions, after which he will start his examination-in-chief. Mr. Tapuskovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mrkovic. You know that I represent Dragomir Milosevic. We have talked at length these days. I'm going to try and be as efficient as possible, and I'm going to try and bring the examination-in-chief to a speedy end because I understand you have to be back home in Serbia because of your previous commitments. Therefore, I'll try and be as efficient as possible. Sir, can you tell us your name for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Ljuban Mrkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 28th of December, 1953?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ljubinje in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed elementary school in Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed the high school for officers in Rajlovac, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed military academy in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The command staff academy that you completed was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict, you worked at military academy as an officer and a teacher?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Rajlovac, in the aeronautical academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict you were captain first class?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you did on the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, 1992, pursuant to a decision of the Supreme Command, together with the former JNA, I withdrew from territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am duty-bound to draw your attention to the transcript. Please make a pause after my question and try to speak slowly, so as every word you say can be recorded. After you did what you did on the 19th of May, 1992, and since you were in Sarajevo, can you tell us what was happening in Sarajevo and in Rajlovac where you were before the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: While the JNA was functioning in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means up to the 19th of May, 1992, the army was engaged in its business. One could feel ethnic tensions among the members of the army. We in Rajlovac, on our strength had Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. Life was normal, the way it had always been, but a moment came when some of the Muslim officers went to the BiH army side. The others remained with us. The same happened to the Croats. Some of them stayed with us. There were constant attacks on Rajlovac, where I worked, from the place called Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, can we take these things slowly. When the problems arose, what was your engagement before you left Sarajevo? What was connected to your rank? What did you do at the time? What was your duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I was engaged at the airport of Butmir, and I was working on the evacuation of the population of Sarajevo. I organised flights at the airport of Butmir, from which the largest number of the population was evacuated from the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly how many people were evacuated and what was the situation like during those times. Can you give us an approximate number of the people who left Sarajevo with your assistance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that we organised daily take-offs of some ten transport aeroplanes AN-26 that could hold up to 35 people, and the aeroplane known as Kikas, Boeing 737, which flew the Belgrade-Sarajevo route almost every day and could hold up to 400 people. On average, nearly 1.000 citizens of Sarajevo were evacuated every day from that airport. I would like to emphasise that at that airport nobody paid attention to the ethnicity. Whoever presented themselves at the airport would be flown to Belgrade and elsewhere. I wasn't in Belgrade. I was in Sarajevo, but I can vouch for the fact that nobody paid any attention to the ethnicity. Everybody was transported, whoever wanted to be evacuated from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate duration of the time when you were doing that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I was doing this from April to June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please wait. Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This lasted from the first take-off, which was on the 9th of April. I can remember this very well. It was a passenger plane by Air Bosna. We asked for this plane to be removed for security reasons, and it lasted up to the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 19th of May you withdrew pursuant to an order, just like every other soldier did. Did you ever return to Sarajevo after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Belgrade. I spent some ten days there, and then I wanted to go back to Sarajevo, to the place where I had resided, to where my family was, to the place where I was born. It was my decision to go back and to stay there. I thought this was the right thing to do, to go back to the place where I had lived all my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the honourable Judges, in the place where you were, were there any other professional career officers who had returned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Very few. At that moment, the moment when I returned to Rajlovac and in the territory of the Sarajevo region, there were very few career officers who had returned immediately after the outbreak of conflict. Within the ten next days, maybe two or three officers returned to the territory of Sarajevo after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any foot soldiers of the JNA who did not hail from Sarajevo who remained in the territory after the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by foot soldiers? I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew on the 19th of May, not only officers withdrew.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The active troops left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned, as you say you did, who did you join?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the units that had already been organised, the Territorial Defence of the Serbian people who had organised those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the combatants in that army that you joined at that moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This was people, volunteers, who volunteered to make the troops. The reserve officers of the former Territorial Defence which automatically became active-duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what happened to the heavy weaponry of the JNA that had been in the territory where you were before you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the weaponry that could be pulled out within such a short deadline and was transported towards Serbia, more specifically, the unit that I was attached to which was the air force academy, we pulled out some of the weaponry, some of the arms that we thought might be necessary in some other location for the training of our students. And some of the equipment and weapons remained in Rajlovac because we had not been in a position to transport them to wherever we were going. It was impossible for us to do that, to transport everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you remember, what pieces remained in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I eye-witnessed the moment when we were withdrawing from Rajlovac; I'm talking about the organised, regular army. As soon as we left Rajlovac, different formations broke into the barracks in Rajlovac, either Serbs or Muslims, and they were taking whatever they deemed necessary. A lot of food was left behind, a lot of ammunition. There was very little weapons anyway because this was a training centre, a school. They also took some mock weapons that we used in training, but this could not be used in combat. Those were just training, teaching aids.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay so this was in Rajlovac, the place where you worked with students. However, did you notice that the army that you joined subsequently did have a certain quantity of heavy weaponry in the place where you served?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have. In any case, they did have maybe not heavy weaponry, but they had infantry weaponry. In Rajlovac, we had never had heavy weaponry, and the situation continued. During the war after I returned from Serbia, we never had any heavy weaponry in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer, but I'm asking you not only about Rajlovac because Ilidza is close by and so is Hadzici. Did you notice in these areas that there was heavy weaponry there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was some heavy weaponry there. There were, I believe, two tanks, T-55 tanks and there were a few howitzers, as far as I can remember. The Republika Srpska army in the territory did have some heavy weaponry, and also there was some heavy weaponry on the side of the BiH army. Those weapons had been taken away from the Marsal Tito barracks, and there was a lot more of them because what could be taken from Rajlovac was just teaching aids, whereas in the barracks there had been a lot more weaponry and that's why they had a lot more than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a good time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're perfectly right. So we're going to take the break now, and we're going to resume in 20 minutes' time. The hearing is closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue, Mr. Mrkovic. In order for us to keep discussing the topic further, I wanted to show you a map. It is 2829, from the 65 ter list, and perhaps we can indicate a few things on it for the Judges. Can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you find the place you returned to, the place where you had been before the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This map is quite small, but I think Rajlovac is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please put a circle there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, you have to be given a pen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark it with an R.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the yellow and red lines represent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The two lines represent the lines of separation between the territory held by the VRS and the Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when were you at that place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: After I returned from Belgrade until the Dayton Peace Accords in January 1996 -- no, December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell Their Honours what exactly was there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the aeronautical institute ORAO, next to the barracks in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Put a circle where the barracks was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to have it located. This is where the barracks was, and next to it there was the institute, adjacent to the barracks. That's where the ORAO facility was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about its geographical location concerning the environs of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The aeronautical institute ORAO and the Rajlovac barracks were at the foot of Sokolje and Zuc, which was constantly under the control of the ABiH. ORAO itself, and the place where I slept at the time, was perhaps 800 metres away from the trenches controlled by the ABiH throughout the conflict. The situation was such, the lines of separation did not move. They were established in 1992, and preserved until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell Their Honours what was done within the institute called ORAO at the time. Was it in operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the conflict it kept repairing jet engines; jet engines, not aeroplane engines. These engines were intended for Serbia and Banja Luka and also for export. We worked for other clients, those who wanted their jet engines maintained or fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The production of those jet engines survived throughout the war. You had a production line, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I add another thing about the institute. The institute was at the foot of Zuc and Sokolje. In my unit where I was the head of security, 24 members of the aeronautical institute were killed and 70 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us discuss something else before that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you're already on the topic, tell me this: During the combat activities was the institute itself in any danger, as such?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was attacked from infantry weapons, but never from artillery. The reason for this was that it was very valuable and profitable. The equipment that was there was of great value, both sides considered it a great achievement to have it under its control. We had security information showing that the ABiH kept insisting in its orders not to target the institute with heavy weaponry because it had nothing to do with the combat readiness of the VRS. These were merely jet engines for planes sent to various Arab countries and all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for such behaviour of the ABiH to try and keep the institute safe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was clear. They were hoping that one day they were going to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which weapons did they use then? Please wait for my question to be complete. Which weapons did they use?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Solely from infantry weapons and snipers, because then in that case there was no damage to the institute itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, please continue what you began saying. Were there any casualties of such firing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Facts are that we had 24 killed and around 70 wounded in the institute during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people soldiers or the workers of the institute?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: These were our workers from the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we are still on the map and to conclude with it, I wanted to ask you if you know something about certain elevations dominating in the area of Sarajevo. Do you know who -- whose forces were at those locations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Rajlovac and its environs, as well as in Ilidza and Vogosca, the main elevations that were there were controlled by the ABiH, starting with Zuc, Sokolje, Rajlovac, and the Rajlovac barracks. They had all those in the palm of their hand. Hum was another important elevation for the city of Sarajevo and it was also controlled by the forces of the ABiH. Igman as well, Trebevic or parts of Trebevic. We only had the territory up to the road, and it was very difficult to move about there. And moving from Vogosca and Rajlovac to Pale was difficult. We always moved along the separation line, and we sustained many losses en route, many people killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell Their Honours something about when you returned to Rajlovac. Besides working in the factory, as you said, what other jobs did you have in terms of military events?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the aeronautical institute was part of the former JNA and then the VRS, I was engaged in security and intelligence efforts in the area of the institute and in the territory around it, including Rajlovac and it environs. I was the security organ chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you belong to any particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Territorially speaking, we were within the AOR of the command of the SRK. We were not attached to any brigades. We were one of the units of the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your job as a security officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: My job as the security officer in the institute was to protect, preserve, the property and personnel of the institute itself, gathering intelligence information and forwarding those up the chain of command and control so that they could make their decisions properly. There was another aspect of activity aimed at preserving the documentation that existed in the aeronautical institute concerning the maintenance of such engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the work of your service? What did it look like, if you can explain?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The service worked like any other service. We were organised as part of the security service of the VRS, and for a while I personally was subordinated to the command along the expert line of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I just wanted to know about the actual work. When you say intelligence security work, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, tell us about your service.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: You would have to take all possible measures, all available measures, in order to protect the aeronautical institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the characteristic of the intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gist of it was that we could not permit the other side to have its people within the institute and to get their hands on information or data of the aeronautical institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you if you knew if any other intelligence services were operating there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo area was very interesting for all intelligence services, the Croatian one, the intelligence service of the B&H army, and the majority of other intelligence services in that area were interested and were present in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed the duty of commander of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the beginning of the conflict there were heavy weapons left behind by the JNA. Do you know what happened to these heavy weapons in 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, all the heavy weapons from the Sarajevo area were withdrawn in accordance to an agreement out of an exclusion zone around Sarajevo of some 20 kilometres. I know all the heavy weapons were pulled out and placed under the control of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please say something about that, since you were there in the area from 1992 until 1995. Can you tell us whether during that time-period there were periods when it was easier to live, when the intensity of the combat was lower?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that the summer, starting from May 1994 until the summer May 1995, in the Sarajevo theatre, was very quiet in terms of armed clashes. This was a period that was characteristic by very, very few combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about after May 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Since we did a lot of intelligence work in that area in order to protect ourselves and preserve ourselves, the people, the property, we had information that in that period, forces under the control of Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out intensive training and preparations, and all of this indicated to us that one day there will be a major offensive in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you this: Did you receive information about things that were happening in that part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the B&H army relating to combat actions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we received information in various ways with the departure of a certain number of the population from Sarajevo, areas that were under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We received information that the communications -- from communications also of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we were quite, quite aware of the situation in the town itself. Also, the other side was aware of what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't just thinking of that. Were you able to receive information through the media or in some other way about the consequences of the combat actions in Sarajevo that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the area that was under the control of the -- and where the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was situated? Were there any consequences in that area as a result of combat between the two sides, as a result of mutual firing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: We had regular analysis about what was going on and what the effects were in the town itself. This was an activity that was carried out routinely, and the media propaganda had a lot to do with everything. I, myself, frequently heard on the media already in the papers, which we got in different ways, that such and such a person was killed on their way out of Sarajevo, whereas in that location not even a shell fell nor was there any firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You as the security service or anyone from the Army of Republika Srpska, did you do anything to check these reports, to find out what happened, to investigate? Was this possible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: We received instructions many times about how to behave in a situation like that. We reported to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska several times that the shells that were dropping in the Sarajevo area, we would ask them to form joint commissions to check if they fell where they fell and so on, but this was never granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm going to show you document DD002492.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, can we just save this map as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to tender this or you want to save it on the registrar list?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to have that admitted as an exhibit, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is being tendered. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes D302.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe I'm missing something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the Prosecutor is on his feet. What's going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It says here: "I'm going to show you a document --" I see, I see, the admission refers to the previous admission of map. I'm sorry, I have no objection, of course, to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear that the exhibit was given a number, but it doesn't matter. If it wasn't given a number, I'm not going to insist on this in order not to burden the Court anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we have the document. Mr. Mrkovic, could you please read the heading, the date of the document, and read up until the actual text begins, and then I'm going to tell you what you need to pay attention to.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit hard for me to see, but the top I can see better. "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kakanj, strictly confidential number 01-1/17-1, dated January 1st, 1995." "Agreement on the cessation of hostilities with guide-lines, to:"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at paragraph 2, please, the third passage of that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is very hard to see. Some things have been crossed out, but perhaps we can place a cleaner page on the ELMO, and then the witness would be able to read what it says. And perhaps we could zoom in a little bit on the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's something like: I forbid ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where it begins: "I forbid ..." Please read from there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "I forbid, and UNPROFOR is to be informed of this, Chetnik officers -- Chetnik liaison officers to be located in UNPROFOR barracks on our territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
