utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph 2, the very last passage, where it says: "There can be no backing away ... " And then further down.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot see very well. "There can be no backing down and talk," I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I please read this to the witness and I am able to read this. There is a translation in English. The interpreters are unable to see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So after the first part that you read it says: "There can be no backing away from that -- there may be no departure from this because I do not want UNPROFOR to legalise in that way the stay of Chetnik liaison officers on our territory, and thereby also their intelligence activities." Well, I have shown you this, you can see that for yourself. Did that have anything to do with your attempts to do something in order to find out about the matters that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, we did know that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not want us to come and to investigate anything or to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm asking you to look at page 2, and to see who issued this order.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This order was issued by commander army general Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now that we're speaking about the document, can you please look at the paragraph just above the signature and can you please read it, I think that you can read it, it's possible. It's on page 2 right above the -- or right below where it says, "commander army general Rasim Delic."

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Corps commander will continue to maintain the full level of combat-readiness and they must not permit any surprises."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And continue, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "If the agreement is respected, use the time to train troops, units, and commands to transform the army, and to prepare to continue combat actions."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is what you talked about earlier. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document DD002492 be tendered as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This being admitted. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you now please tell me if you knew anything about there being a tunnel beneath the Butmir airport; and if you do, can you please tell me what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the translation here, so I don't see -- oh, all right, very well. When the tunnel began -- well, when the excavations for the tunnel began, we knew about it. We knew when that was completed and when the tunnel began to be used. It was used for regrouping of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also it was used as an exit from the area that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was also used for food and the supply of other items. It was very much used. We were informed that it operated continuously 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information that had to do with the tunnel and weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the data we had, there was specific times when civilians were able to use the tunnel, that was for a very short period of time, and the rest of the time was for the needs of the military. The tunnel was used to bring in and take out troops, so troops came in and left Sarajevo via the tunnel. And weapons in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question was not written down. I didn't turn my microphone on. What about the weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Weapons, too. Yes, the tunnel was definitely used for the traffic of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you document DD002743, and when you have the document in front of you can you please look at the heading of the document and then further down. And can you please then give me an answer to a question. I believe this is more legible. Please read out the heading.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Command of the 102nd Brigade, strictly confidential number 16/1-52, 27 April, 1995. "Relief of units in the zone of responsibility of the 16th Land Army Division order. "On the basis of the planned use of the units in the area of responsibility of the 16th DKOV and the order for the relief of units issued by the command of the 12th division, strictly confidential number 02/2-11-20, dated 25 April 1995, and in order to prepare the units in due course for carrying out combat tasks outside the Sarajevo theatre, I order: "Prepare forces out of the 3rd bb, the strength of a battalion (400 soldiers and officers) to relieve the 1/102nd bbr in the area of responsibility of the 16th Division and take the position and its area of defence. Relieve the units on the 3rd of May 1995 by 1600 hours. "Out of the 3rd bb, use: 280 soldiers, including three squads for the 60-millimetre MB and one squad for the 82-millimetre MB" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this something you had information on? Did you refer to it a while ago?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a regular activity which often took place. I specified how the tunnel was designated primarily for military purposes and there was only a short window for the movement of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that DD002743 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's being admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, you mentioned the weapons transported through the tunnel. What was your information on the arming of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The Army of BiH had large quantities of weapons left behind by the former JNA, primarily those from the Marsal Tito barracks in the area where I was. Then there was another large warehouse at Busovaca, then from Zenica, Busovaca, and so on and so forth. During the war we had information that the Army of BiH through various channels got its supplies from abroad, from various Arab countries, and that weapons were being brought in on planes, as well as in humanitarian convoys which made their way through to Sarajevo. MR. TAPUSKOVIC; [Intepretation] Let us show DD003643 to the witness, please. It reflects a session of the Presidency of the Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina, chaired by Alija Izetbegovic on the 10th of August, 1995; i.e., in the period pertaining to the indictment. The document is DD003643. Your Honours, I had a portion of these minutes translated, and I wanted to show the witness parts of it. Once it is on the screen, I would ask the witness to read out the heading and the time when -- and date when the session began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please try and make the effort.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 10 August 1995." "The session commenced at 1200 hours." "The session was chaired by President of the Presidency of the RBH, Alija Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to page 6 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English, please. That has been translated. The paragraph beginning with the words: "You see ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to start reading from the bottom of the page, saying: "In the last 15 days, we ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, almost the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "In the past 15 days, we brought in 26 aircraft-loads of weapons." I transferred them. "Does anyone know who brought them in? Do the people know who did that? These are completely unknown people. 26 aircraft-loads of weapons. The man who came was in Germany, the wounded one, he was wounded for two years."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the next page. It is page 7 in the B/C/S and still page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This thing beginning with Catic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Catic, he saw the army in 1992. He's now back and says: You can no longer recognise this army, this one is a real army, the one before was not. Those were just groups of unarmed men. Now it is a well-armed and trained army. We did it all. This was not done by the government. A part of it was done by the government, but a lot ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to page 5. Let's see who the person who said this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does it say at the top?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "President."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to page 10, and in the English it is page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph towards the bottom. It says: "Bace" [phoen] in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "There is a mention of 26 planes which arrived in the last few days if it has to do with 10.000 VBR rockets, 10.000 AR rockets," I don't know what it means, "800 air-bombs, et cetera, then I can say" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to page 9 to see whose words these are. Towards the bottom, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It says "President."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Silajdzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to make things complete, let us go to page 11, which is page 8 in the English, the words uttered by Silajdzic, the beginning of that portion. Page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The words of Silajdzic: "If the ratio ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "If the ratio is 90:10, it means that we have received a billion and a half or 2 billion weapons. Then I don't know. If this is the ratio. Because I can openly say that I initiated and asked for it at a time when you reproached me for it, asked me why I needed these weapons, when they were transported to Turkey on my request, if you remember. And we both said: We might need weapons. Including this. I can safely say between $70 and $80 million. Later on this was sent here from Turkey."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And another thing on page 13, beginning with Silajdzic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out loud Silajdzic's words, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "Let us say who the people are who work and believe me, they aren't, either" -- I'm having difficulty reading this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do your best, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "I know more or less who these people are. More power to them. I know these men and you don't. I can tell you about men who didn't sleep for nights on end, loading cargo on ships in far-away countries. Their names will never be known. They were both our citizens and so on, and when you talk about the 26 latest planes, with those 26 planes, if you please" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is good enough, since you are having some difficulty reading. Is this the information that reached you during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've no objection to this document coming in because we have had so many documents with the same very, very tiny foundation linked to this witness. All he did was reading out large portions of what other people said in other meetings he didn't attend, and at the end the normal question: Does that correspond to what you have seen? What I'd love to see was this gentleman's analysis, perhaps, an intelligence report of that time which would confirm his intrinsic knowledge, I'm sure, he had of the ABiH. But anyway, that's the way it is. I've no objection to the document being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as any intelligence person, he knew of this. I know of no intelligence service in the world that would have within its system the possibility of putting all the information they receive on paper and reporting on it all. They only do it in a most delicate, subtle way, as explained by the witness. He can explain to us how an intelligence service works. He explained about this, and he mentioned these facts discussed by the Presidency of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the president, by Silajdzic, and by the supreme commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic. I did not want to bother you with Delic's statements in this document as well as the statements of others. But from that you would be able to see the pride they were taking in their well-armed army by that time. After all the intelligence information this witness has gathered, I see no reason to refuse the tendering of this document because he had all that information at his disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will admit the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to rush, Witness, and I wanted to ask you this: Concerning combat activities of both parties, of course you can tell us about things happening on both sides, but I'm interested in knowing whether you as intelligence people had some information on the weaknesses or poor state of -- or the poor state of maintenance of weaponry on the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: There were on both sides, since the Army of BiH as well as the VRS will organise the way they were because of the lack of training on both sides. There were often occurrences in which people inflicted wounds on themselves because they were poorly trained and then ordnance would explode, and then sometimes there was friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a document, this being DD002659, it is a very short document. I'd like to ask you to read out the whole thing and then provide an answer to a question of mine. Can you read what it says here so that I can ask you questions about what you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "B&H army, 12th Division command, logistics section. "Strictly confidential 07/24-3-605. "Sarajevo, 17th of June 1995," and it's being sent to the command of the 1st Corps technical service. "Pursuant to the document of the 101st Mountain Brigade command number 5138, dated 16th of June 1995, two 120-millimetre shells marked UP 01/94 7SF09 were fired. The firing was executed in 1140 and 1540 hours. Immediately after being fired from the mortar barrel, the shell dropped in front on the ground some 4 to 5 metres away and did not explode. They have another nine shells with the same marking. Besides these, they also have some 120-millimetre mortar shells marked 95-03-4 whose charges are damp. "Please take the necessary measures to repair them at the authorised Pretis workshop. "Commander Fikret Prevljak."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this what you said earlier about how you found out about these things, about mines dropping on one's own positions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Whether because of the human factor or some technical glitches, but this did used to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please tender this document, DD002659 as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is admitted. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your security intelligence services, did they sometimes find out perhaps even more sensitive and unpleasant information that would be facing the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that in Sarajevo - when I say "Sarajevo," I also mean the areas held both by the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we're talking about Sarajevo and there were different happenings there. Primarily, I'm thinking about some things that were covered by the media. Did you have any information in that sense in relation to those media events which were particularly emphasised by the media?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I said before that the media very frequently published items about shells falling and killing people, whereas later we would find out through the intelligence sources we had within town that none of that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were any events announced sometimes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were. Frequently, they would announce their attacks to us. I can openly say that in 90 per cent of the cases we knew about all the offensives and attacks that were going to be carried out by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. Unfortunately, they also knew about ours, but that's how the system functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like you to pay particular attention to the following document: DD001825. And can you carefully read again here the heading and a good part of the text on that page, and then I could draw your attention to a few sentences. This is in quite large letters. If you are able to, can you, please, carefully read everything that is on this page.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "General Staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Staff of the army headquarters of the army number 1-1/1120-1, Kakanj, the 26th of August, 1995. "Special information to the command of the 1st Corps. "We are forwarding herewith a document of the office of security services with new data on the intentions of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In regard to the above, take immediate measures, all measures that are required, operations and procedures in regard to command number 1/1116-1, dated 25th of August, 1995. "Chief of Staff, General Enver Hadzihasanovic." And then below it says: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Internal Affairs, office of security services, Sarajevo, special information, number 95, dated 25th of August, 1995. "Official secret, strictly confidential, copy number 2. "Command of the so-called Sarajevo-Romanija Corps has issued a command on full combat-readiness and the undertaking of planned counter measures in the next two days for the purpose of breaking the blockade by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." I don't know if it says here -- "to break the blockade of Sarajevo," exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at page 2. We don't need to read everything; there is no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please, this part beginning with: "In connection with that ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please help me where that is because I do not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the second sentence, Mr. Mrkovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: "In connection with the stated command relating also to the use of artillery weapons according to the already-marked and pre-determined points in the depth because when it is put in place it will stop, based on which we have established that in the coming two days the Chetniks intend to shell civilian buildings in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at the last sentence of that text on that part of the page. No, no, the last sentence, Mr. Mrkovic, begins with: "Based on ..." Is it possible that you cannot see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it. It's very hard for me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the last sentence, begins with: "Based on these and previous ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can zoom in on that. This is very important for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problem if the Defence would like to read the sentence out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me. Had I known that you don't see to such an extent, Mr. Mrkovic, I would have provided some glasses for you. I'm going to read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Tapuskovic, that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Based on these and prior information, we believe that the Serb terrorists will over the next few days fire from artillery projectiles of major destructive power at the town of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was the 25th of August when this document was drafted. At the time, did you have any indications that anything was being prepared and were you more cautious because of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony I said that this was a period of truce, but that throughout the time the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was conducting preparations, training to continue combat actions. We received much, much information from the town of Sarajevo, how and in which way this training was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying this is the 25th of August, 1995. What happened on the 26th of August, 1995, and what happened on the 28th of August, 1995, Witness?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was that what was being indicated here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: All this information indicated that something along those lines would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This was signed by Nedzad Ugljen, and it was dispatched to the president, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic; the command of the Main Staff, Mr. Rasim Delic; and to the minister of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Mr. Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out over that time over those few days if Alija Izetbegovic was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: We found out from the media that Alija -- or we were receiving information that Alija was going to leave Sarajevo. And I can say that care was always taken care. Igman was never fired at because that's where they passed, and that is when Alija appeared, according to all indications, in Mostar, some two or three days before Markale. The president was in Mostar two or three days before Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this concern you a bit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Just like any analysts, we did carry out a lot of analyses about the events, events in Sarajevo. Something terrible would always happen when the leadership was not in Sarajevo. Large attacks would take place when the leadership was not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you please look and tell us who signed this.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Nedzad Ugljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Nedzad Ugljen is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of State Security in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know to which units he belonged to? Was there a special unit that he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: He was in the State Security Service of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a document that the army took from the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document tendered as a Defence exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The document is admitted. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how much time I have in order to be able to keep track. I'm not really keeping control here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 15 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your intelligence service, did it have information about any irregular actions undertaken by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at any point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Just like any service, sometimes we would receive accurate and sometimes we would receive false information. Extraordinary situations were happening all the time. Practically every situation for us was an extraordinary situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were there any unusual actions in such conditions? I'm not permitted to suggest anything.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very frequently it would happen that various shells were fired at our positions, shells of contents unknown to us that dropped on our positions. I don't know exactly which part to mention, for example, which section.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't understand my question, I'm not permitted to suggest anything to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you said that there was a year of -- there was a lull for a year.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: From May 1994 to May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And so what started to happen in May 1995? Do you know of any events, incidents in May 1995? Was any combat conducted then that you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically in the area where I was there were many provocations that already started from May 1995. All the information indicated that the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were preparing to lift the blockade of the town, that they were preparing to attack along all the lines of the front, and we were also preparing for that throughout the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "the so-called lifting of the siege," and it was not registered like that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that anything happened in May around a barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an attack on the Bosut barracks, I think, up there on Trebevic. Many, many shells landed on that barracks then. There were a number of our soldiers killed and wounded. I know that that barracks was often attacked and particularly fiercely so in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I want to show you another document now, which is DD002681. Please have a look at the document. Have a look at the date, and after some cursory reading I want to ask you if what is mentioned here is the same thing you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, this is the amount of ammunition spent, fired at Bosut on Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the amount of ammunition spent, can you have a look at the last three items?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Mine 60-millimetre, 516 pieces; 82-millimetre shells, 507; 120-millimetre shells, 74 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please explain to us why you would like this document to be admitted. What are you trying to establish by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have discussed this on many occasions before, and you have admitted similar documents. The intensity of combat activities on the part of the ABiH is the very reason for the mutual actions at that time. I already explained my arguments. I can do it yet again, but until now we have admitted at least ten such documents which have never been disputed. This is a document reflecting the beginning of that offensive with the intensive activities on the ABiH side. The number of casualties following such activities is a good indication of the intensity of combat actions by the ABiH. Therefore, one cannot speak of a campaign or terror that was supposed to have result; rather, it was an unavoidable answer to combat activities in the course of fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Is in the transcript and the Chamber will admit this document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I intended to use another few documents, but I don't want to repeat myself. I wish to thank you for the time allotted to me, and I have no further questions for this witness. I would like to thank Mr. Mrkovic and Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. You finished before the break. According to my calculations, you had 20 more minutes, so I congratulate you. And in order not to waste any more time, Mr. Waespi has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and if the Defence agrees, I will take their 20 minutes and add them to my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I tried to be funny. I will try to be as brief as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I'm still not quite sure what your association was within the chain of command of either the SRK or the VRS. I believe at one time you said you were for a period of time within the professional chain of command of the SRK security, and at other times you told us that you were working for the VRS Main Staff. So please tell us, for the period of time you came back to Belgrade -- to Rajlovac from Belgrade, which I take it is somewhere end of May 1992, to the end of the war, November 1995, who was your superior at any time? Can you please let us know in as much detail as you can.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon my return to the aeronautical institute at Rajlovac, my direct superior in all matters was the general manager of the institute. I was his security assistant in terms of the institute. The aeronautical institute ORAO was a unit of the VRS subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS, directly under it. However, since we were within the AOR of the SRK, in terms of professional subordination concerning logistics and support, we relied on the SRK. That is what the system was like in the VRS at the time. I believe I was as clear in my first explanation as now -- as I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know who Marko Lugonja is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, chief of security of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you working with him during the relevant period, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked with him on issues of security at the institute and in Rajlovac, and most of the information I forwarded was through or to Marko Lugonja. That was because, as I mentioned, we were within the AOR where he was chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I understand you correctly, you were not formally subordinated to Marko Lugonja or the SRK?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you exchanged information with him in a professional sense, like intelligence --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- And other relevant information for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, let's very briefly talk about 1992. I guess we disagree forever who started the war in -- around Sarajevo, and there were experts -- there will be experts from the Defence side on this issue. But the reason why civilians, the population, part of the population, left Sarajevo in April, May, June 1992, and you explained how you helped organising that, was the relentless bombardment of the city of Sarajevo by JNA and, indeed, the VRS once a transformation has been executed. Could we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot. I don't think that the bombardment was so relentless. In April 1992, there was infantry combat, and as far as I know and as far as I could hear in 1992, there was no use of heavy weaponry. To be specific, in Rajlovac and at the airport where we were, what was there was infantry weapons. As for any heavy weapons in April 1992, I don't think there were any -- at least I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In May, mid-May 1992, 14th of May, the situation was so bad inside the city that UNHCR had to pull out of the city. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was at the Butmir airport. We were trying to pull out the planes from there. I don't know whether it was so indeed. We heard of people leaving Sarajevo, of some panic, firing. Well, everyone tried to flee; that is the truth. As for any shelling, I cannot say there was none but I cannot say there was either. I wasn't the person who observed it or headed the whole thing, but I think the shelling was -- was made to sound too important than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It was certainly important enough and painful enough, the shelling, that Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade was telling French UNPROFOR General Morillon that the bombardment of Sarajevo was, and I quote him: "Bloody common criminal" and that there was no "justification for the continued bombardment of the civilian population of Sarajevo." That was the 30th of May, 1992. Do you think that's an accurate description of what was happening in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: As a professional soldier, I would call any shelling of anyone a crime. I would be very much against it. But by that time the front lines had been established. We were all trying to save our hides. I was always against illegal use of fire-power, and we always insisted on not responding too strongly. However, there is a fact that needs to be recognised, and I'm trying to cut things short since I have many obligations to attend to in Belgrade. Both the VRS and the Army of the Federation were very untrained. The only army that knew anything about waging wars had withdrawn by that time. The Muslim officers did not want to go to the front. I knew some of the colleagues of mine, we would hug and kiss and he would go back to Sarajevo and I went to Belgrade crying. We were all fleeing the same war, but once there we realised that there was nowhere to go, that we had to go back. Both those in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and we in the VRS were poorly trained for such events. And it caused certain results on both sides. In any case, I condemn any shelling. As an air force officer, I was in charge of organising the withdrawal of people from Sarajevo. At no moment did we pay any heed to who was what, Muslims, Serbs, or Croat, we were pulling them out as they came. People used to give them their cars just so they would be able to flee, and everyone fled. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether the description of General Morillon and, indeed, President Milosevic, when they condemned the bombardment, the continued bombardment of the civilian population of Sarajevo in May 1992, whether that was correct or whether you disagree that there was heavy bombardment of the civilian population in Sarajevo from Serb forces around Sarajevo, whether you disagree with that or whether you accept that description. I'm happy to show you the document which records very briefly the conversation between General Morillon and Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me to say that there was shelling, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whoever this has to do with, I'm not trying to exaggerate on anyone's importance, but this witness cannot speak on anything someone else said, be it Milosevic or Morillon. I think it would only be fair to ask the witness what he knows, what he saw, what he experienced. It is far more important than any of Milosevic's statements or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is an intelligence officer and he was there at that time, and he is -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, Slobodan Milosevic, who is now in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Who was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not in Sarajevo. This gentleman, however, was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like it to be written in the transcript verbatim as the Defence counsel just mentioned it. Very well. I notice that it is time to take a break. We will stop now, and we'll take a 20-minute break. A 20-minute break. The hearing is suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be surprised to see me, but -- but why should a little cold and flu keep me away from -- from company and the setting that I find so agreeable. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand you're cross-examining, and there was to be a ruling on an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to a conversation between Slobodan Milosevic and General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR general where they talk about the bombardment of the city of Sarajevo in May 1992, and this was in response to the witness's answer who said he can neither confirm nor deny that there was bombardment in Sarajevo. And my learned friend Tapuskovic said how can this witness, you know, talk about something -- a meeting in Belgrade. But my point is because the witness gave his answer not responsive about the situation in Sarajevo and he was in Sarajevo and he talked about the situation. I should be entitled to put my case to the witness, famous paragraph 7, where we talk about bombardment of the city in 1992. And this document, I'm sure, assists Your Honours and perhaps might refresh the witness's recollection of what was happening in Sarajevo in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, what are you seeking from this witness? What is this witness to do or to say in relation to the conversation between Mr. Milosevic and the other person about the bombardment of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness was asked in chief about his involvement of getting the civilian population out of Sarajevo, and I asked the witness why. And he didn't really give an answer, so I was putting to him that one of the reasons why the civilian population was fleeing Sarajevo was because of the shelling by the VRS, JNA, before they pulled out of Sarajevo. And then the witness gave the answer: "I cannot say there was none and I cannot say there was either." So in order to, number one, refresh his recollection of what was happening before his eyes in Sarajevo; and number two, about his credibility. I would like to show him this brief document which is very, very straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what does the document say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It says -- in fact, you see it in front of you. It says that General Morillon complained to General Milosevic about the shelling of Sarajevo and said he should use his influence with General Mladic to stop the bombardment of Sarajevo. And then he said, Milosevic said, while he could: "... understand fighting in self-defence, there was no justification for the continued bombardment of the civilian population of Sarajevo. This was, moreover, not in the interests of Yugoslavia nor the Bosnian Serbs." This is Milosevic saying that. So that shows that not only the leading UNPROFOR general in Sarajevo says there was a bombardment of civilian population in May 1992, but also Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade. The witness was there and I would like to know whether he accepts that there was bombardment of civilian population in Sarajevo or not. That's my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's almost a step ahead because I haven't shown the document yet to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, Witness, if you could read the second paragraph of this document which you see on your screen. The Serbian version is on the right side. You see it's a communication from UNPROFOR General Nambiar to New York, and he talks about a meeting held on the 30th May 1992, between President Slobodan Milosevic and, among others, Generals Morillon, MacKenzie, and Auger. And the second part, the second paragraph, talks about, and I've quoted that two or three times, about the "continued bombardment of civilian population of Sarajevo." And later in paragraph 3, it talks -- it's an assessment of Slobodan Milosevic and he calls it a "bloody, criminal bombardment." So my question to you, Witness, is: Do you accept that there was shelling of the civilian population in Sarajevo by forces under General Mladic? If you can answer, yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, before this Trial Chamber I have made a solemn declaration to speak the truth and nothing but the truth. I'm saying that there was no shelling in Butmir and Rajlovac airports where I was. War was going on within the town and in other locations. I can only speculate. What I'm saying here is only the truth; where I was, there was no shelling. Whatever else I might say, if I said there was or wasn't, this would be very arbitrary on my part. I did not command any units. I did not issue any orders. Please do not ask me whether there was any shelling elsewhere because I was not involved. My wife was in Sarajevo as well as my children in the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard. Your answer is that you can speak to Butmir and Rajlovac and you can say there was no shelling in those areas in the airports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you told us you were involved in helping civilians from the city of Sarajevo boarding aeroplanes. Didn't these people tell you what they endured in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: If all hundred civilians pass by you and they all look disturbed and if your task is to organise their exit from Sarajevo, to organise planes to put them on, then you don't have the time to talk to them. I was in a very difficult position, but you could see on their faces that something was going on and that is a fact, I admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the document could be admitted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Biljana Plavsic is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know that even she was complaining that there was shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo in May 1992. Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what -- something said and nothing surprises me. Why should it surprise me? What I am saying is that I am telling you about the things I know. As for what Biljana said, what Milosevic said, that's an entirely different matter. Maybe they were privy to some other information. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Let's move away from 1992, in a few other areas you discussed. If we could pull up Defence Exhibit 303, please. I'm sure you recall the -- I think the first document you were -- or one of the first documents you were shown. This was a document generated by the BH General Staff, and it dates of the 1st of January, 1995, and that's a copy which was not very well legible. So let me read just a part you were asked about by Defence. For your convenience it said, and this is on the first point -- on the first page in the middle: "I forbid, and UNPROFOR is to be informed of this, Chetnik liaison officers to be located in UNPROFOR bases on our territory." And it goes on to say: "Let UNPROFOR deploy on their territories or send its liaison officers to both us and them." For whatever reason, you seem to link it to a joint commission to investigate incidents. Nowhere in this document does it say anything about investigation of some incidents. It talks about liaison officers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand this document as a ban on the part of the command of the BiH army, on the presence of any officers in the area, which is corroborated by the document. I've also said that we never shied away from any investigation of any shells, where they came from, how they came from, but throughout the war we were not in a position to investigate. And let me tell you this: The other side was not really keen on proving what was going on in the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. We had just one case that was Markale where we had a joint commission. Two of our officers escorted by UNPROFOR went there, and they returned within two hours. What could they see in two hours? I leave it to you to be the judge of that. So that was just one joint mission and a very short-lived one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Two points. The first one, the document does not talk about offering investigative resources; it talks about the presence of liaison officers on the ABiH territory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Our liaison officers were never there as far as I know. They were not allowed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was: It talks about liaison officers. It does not talk about any investigative steps being carried out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Our liaison officers were not in the territory of BiH army, not that I know of. They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Don't answer this question. Let's move on to these investigative commissions then. Give me, apart from Markale, an example, if you can recall, that a joint --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us just be clear what Markale we are talking about. Was it Markale I or Markale II? When was it allowed for the officers to go there and inspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair point. Thanks, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll come to this Markale I and II in a moment. But apart from those Markale incidents, can you give me an example, if you recall, an example you know first-hand that you offered to UNPROFOR or the ABiH to investigate any incident. Do you remember any such example?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I gave you the -- that one example, and I don't know which Markale was in question. I only know that I often received information about a shell that killed civilians, that a request was made that this should be investigated through UNPROFOR, through liaison officers, but it was simply not possible. They were not allowed to do that. I am sure of that because that's the information that I received. Why was this not allowed? Because very many times the number of victims was exaggerated. For example, news would say a shell fell at Bascarsija, a number of victims was given, and it turned out eventually there was none. I don't know of any cases save for Markale. Maybe one or two more cases were in which our officers went there. I know that requests were made quite often through our liaison officers; that I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, and it's important for me to know at least of one example of these many occasions that you received information about a shell that killed civilians, to quote you. Can you give me, aside from these two Markale incidents, an example when somebody asked you that an incident should be investigated. If you can tell me who the person was that asked you, or somebody else from your office, when it was in relation to what incident.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally never requested that in the territory of Rajlovac because there were very few shells that fell over there. We were such units that did not have any artillery pieces, and I can't tell you who it was who requested that. But I know for sure through conversations, through information that I received, that the liaison officers did ask for the truth to be established. But I'm sure that the liaison officers who was a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps could tell you more about that. He was the one who communicated directly with UNPROFOR and with the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you don't know more -- you don't know anything more about this subject. You suggest that we should --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Another issue you talked about was in relation to Defence Exhibit D306, and you were asked about friendly fire. And I think you volunteered the word that friendly fire occurred on, if I quote you directly, on the ABiH side and on the SRK side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the shells being fired as a result of the lack of training or bad ammunition, and for example, people intended to target something and instead of targeting that, they would fire at their own side. That was a very common occurrence, both in our army and in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I was referring to, friendly fire at their own people. Can you give me an example, since you say that it happened on both sides, one example each for the SRK and one example for the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Very specifically, in my unit during the war at least five people were wounded from fire-arms because of a lack of training. Some shells that fell in the vicinity of our ORAO, those incidents were investigated. They happened in 1994, and they came from our positions. Those shells were fired from our positions and our soldiers were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So these incidents were investigated; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you enlighten us a little bit how this -- if you have any knowledge about that, how such an investigation would look like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: The matter of fact was that we would investigate the origin of every shell that fell. We would look at their serial numbers and if we realised that those were our serial numbers and they fell on our positions, that would mean that they had been fired from our positions. This is what happened in our army, but this happened on the other side as well. All the shells are registered under serial numbers. For example, in the BiH army and in the Serbian army, this happened very often because there was a clear lack of training on both sides. People were not very well trained in using those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you would go and find out where the artillery or mortar piece was, who the gunners were, identify these people, talk to them, interrogate them, offer more training, these kind of steps would normally be initiated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct and this was done regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said also that you have recently received information, and I think your source of information was publication in the media. And you say that you had then your intelligence sources within the city who would say that none of it has really happened. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of such an incident that occurred, perhaps a date, perhaps a casualty alleged in the media, and so we can have a detailed picture of your evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: A concrete example. In 1994, it was published in the media that some ten people were killed in front of a tunnel, including some children. Five days later, a person came with the assistance of UNPROFOR who resided nearby, in the building nearby, who didn't know anything about that. He said that nothing of that sort had happened. This was just propaganda. We did want to know what was going on. We wanted to have accurate information. Not a single professional officer who was there could find justification in anybody firing a shell at civilians. All of us who were there who were professional soldiers would never have ordered that. None of us did, and we would do everything in our power to make sure that such things did not happen. At the end of the day, the international humanitarian war was binding upon us, and all of us officers had to comply with it. Unfortunately, both in the ABiH army and in the Army of Republika Srpska there were very, very few educated officers. And one of the problems in both cases was the fact there were few educated officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to that example, and I would really like to insist in you giving more details, if you can. I know it's a long time ago, but I would like to back up your information with some substance. This incident that you referred to about the killing of some ten people in front of the tunnel, including children, can you tell us the date and also a little bit more about the person, the person who came to you and said: This all didn't happen. Are you able to tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the date, but quite a few people confirmed that from the area of Dobrinja, from the vicinity of that tunnel. But I've told you that this was not an isolated case. There were many such cases that we stopped paying attention to. We just put it down to propaganda, and it was proven, subsequently, that this was all down to the propaganda. That is not forbidden, mind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's what I'm interested in proving. It's not helpful at least for me, I don't know how other people in this courtroom look at it, that you say it happened often. I would like to focus on this one incident in Butmir where people are killed, including children, a very, very seriously allegation. So you can't really help us more about that incident?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that perhaps the incident where NATO later threatened air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend has put a question which contains a reference to the incident where children were killed, and the witness said that, subsequently, it was established that nobody had been killed. In other words, my learned friend is saying something that the witness did not confirm. The witness said that the first piece of information was that children had been killed, and that later, subsequently, it had been proven that they were able to establish through some channels of theirs that nobody had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that lesson in logic, but counsel is allowed to probe a little. And for my part, I don't see anything improper in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you talked about a lull in what was happening in May 1994 to 1995. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that only relates to combat activities. There was lots going on at that time. There was hostage-taking, there was shelling and sniping, there was cutting electricity of the population, there was lots of suffering happening by the civilian population during that lull, as you call it, in combat activity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, again you're asking me to tell you something without any documents, something that I did not eye-witness. If you are saying that civilians suffered, I'm sure that they did because every war brings suffering. However, when it comes to the army and the period of lull that I mentioned, for us that was a good period. After the fighting, the fierce combat, after many dead and wounded, all of a sudden there is a period of lull where nothing is going on. I can't talk about the electricity, water, and things like that because I was not involved in that. We did have information that the other side was getting ready for defence, and we did the same. When you mention suffering, I agree with you, there was a lot of suffering but it's not up to me to talk about the suffering and the causes of the suffering. I'm not competent to talk about that. What I'm competent to say is that during that period we did an overhaul of 25 aeroplanes, which cost a lot of money. I was involved heavily in that. I collected information that helped me do that part of job as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. I just want to make sure that I understand you. When you say that the period was good for you, you don't exclude the possibility that for the civilians inside the city, trapped - and that's the word I use, Defence might disagree - the life was not that good as it was for you in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: There is very little difference, to be honest. In order for me to go from Rajlovac to Pale to buy some food, I had to walk 11 kilometres by the fire -- firing line, and I could be killed at any moment from a stray bullet. We did not have any other route. I don't know how familiar you are with the map - in order to leave Sarajevo we could only go through Mrkonjic and Poljine on a market road and we were always at their side. Whenever we did that, we would go during the night. We dimmed our lights, we drove in the dark. We also suffered -- I'm not saying the people in Sarajevo did not suffer, but we also suffered at the same time. It was war -- wartime. We all suffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just the as a matter of interest, how often did you have to do that walk of 11 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see my wife and children for three and a half months because I didn't dare take that road. I was afraid I might get killed. Every time we wanted to go from Sarajevo to Pale, we took a great risk. And if you're referring to how long it took by car, it took more than an hour to negotiate the 11 kilometres of that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you accept that the VRS leadership, the leadership of the Republika Srpska, used utilities or threatened to use utilities as a means of war? Do you have any information about that, cutting off electricity, gas, water, as a means of war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of the leadership of Republika Srpska doing that. I don't remember. I only know that we did not have electricity in Rajlovac. So, when the town had electricity, we had it as well. And as for water, I don't know whether a tap could be turned off somewhere. Electricity outages were common on both sides; that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, does the indictment make that allegation, that utilities were used as a means of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's part of the Prosecution's case, that part of the terror count was that it was within the ability of the VRS and the SRK and, indeed, the political leadership to stop humanitarian aid into the city by firing at UNHCR/UNPROFOR convoys to cut utilities whenever they wanted. That's part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was asking whether it was in the indictment, or is it just something that you're eliciting through evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly. The indictment is fairly short on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it's clearly within the terror count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not seeking to prevent you. I just want to be clear about it. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, if I may be heard, Your Honours. This is not worded expressly anywhere as a count in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, Mr. President, of the indictment, and I read it out: "Because of the shelling and sniping against civilians, the life of virtually every Sarajevo inhabitant became a daily struggle to survive. Without gas, electricity, or running water, people were forced to venture outside to find basic living necessities, often risking death." And it goes on. So that's a clear indication, Mr. President, that because electricity, gas, water was often cut-off, people had to venture outside their homes, thus risking their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If Exhibit 03420 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this, Witness, is a communication from Viktor Andreev, a UN representative in Sarajevo, to Sergio de Mello who was in Zagreb, and he talks about a meeting between General Rose and the Serb leadership in -- on 20th September 1994. That's during the time you talked about there was a lull in activities. And if I can direct you to the third paragraph which is in the English version right at the end of the page. I can read it slowly for you, perhaps you could follow it also on the B/C/S version, if that could be pulled down a little bit. It says here, and he talks about Karadzic saying something. I quote: "In his words, if the international community treats us like a beast, then we will behave like a beast. He specifically mentioned in this regard, the use of utilities as a means of war. As the afternoon progressed, he mellowed somewhat, indicating that he might consider restoring electricity, water, and gas to Sarajevo if these were done in the context of repairs to utilities in Bosnia as a whole." Now, that suggests that, indeed, the VRS leadership -- the RS leadership was capable of influencing the utilities in Sarajevo. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in charge of the electricity. I wouldn't know how to turn it on and off, so I'm not familiar with the decisions governing that aspect of everything. All I know is that when we had electricity, parts of Sarajevo or Sarajevo also had electricity. But I'm unable to comment on what Karadzic discussed with somebody, whether electricity could be cut-off or switched on and the water is something I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would accept that because of what we see here, what we read here, the civilian population who had no utilities at times because of action of the Republika Srpska, VRS, was suffering, despite the lull described by you in the conflict between May 1994 and 1995. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can agree to the extent that the population in Ilidza, Vogosca, and Sarajevo suffered the same thing. I was not in any better position than the soldier at Zuc. We were in the same position, except he had a way out through the tunnel and I had a way out 12 kilometres along the sniper line of fire. I cannot confirm that somebody had an intention to do that, to cut-off electricity. I don't know about that. But that I had a hard time without water, that is true. Every man in town without water had the same difficulties anywhere. As for if this was done or not, I don't know. For a while there was talk that the Russians were cutting off the gas, but sometimes there was gas and sometimes there wasn't gas. So if we happened to have gas -- Sarajevo also had gas. I think that gas began to arrive in Sarajevo in 1991 or 1992. Excuse me. Just one thing. I agree in one thing. All of us together in the Sarajevo valley suffered, the civilian population, one army, and the other army. We suffered in this way or that way, depends, but we all suffered. I was on the side of the Army of Republika Srpska. I very infrequently went out to Pale or went anywhere, afraid that I would get killed, moving around was difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And I also acknowledge that it was very difficult for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Mr. Waespi, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you cannot confirm that somebody had an intention to do that, "cut-off electricity." But this document says that Karadzic, indeed, had the intention to use electricity, utilities, as a means of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I intended that you should move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move away from that document. The witness has already said he can't comment on the basis of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If it could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 816, Your Honours -- P816.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Another point you mentioned in answer to my question. You said that the people inside Sarajevo could have left Sarajevo through the tunnel. But earlier in answering a question from Defence, you said that mostly the tunnel was used by the military and there was only a small window for civilians. You're not suggesting that every person, every civilian in Sarajevo could have easily moved out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean that every civilian could have easily moved out of Sarajevo through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. What do you say to that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by my previous statement. The exact schedule of when the military could go through and when the civilians could go through. They waited in line to -- for their turn to go out or to come back. It took -- these were two-hour blocks, two hours to go out of Sarajevo, two hours to come in to Sarajevo. And it was a question of what had to be done, priorities, and so on and so forth. And now it's a question of whether everybody wanted to leave Sarajevo. Probably those who wanted to leave were able to leave. Now when I meet with those who were in town, and we were in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, they would say left, went in and out, five or ten times. So it was possible to do that often, and those who wished to leave were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's your basis for information that everybody who wanted to leave Sarajevo through the tunnel could leave the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm providing the information on the basis of data we received from Sarajevo, and at the end of the war when it all stopped. And many, many our colleagues who had remained in Sarajevo talked about how they went out, about the routes they took to come out. So I don't see any reason that this would be information that was not accurate. It's accurate because there's a whole bunch of people, and from conversations even recently, I have information that, for example, there was frequently water at a specific location and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So now you're able to talk about Sarajevo. Previously, you kind of confined your experience to Rajlovac. But why didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness comment on that, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel is saying that apparently you are now able to talk about Sarajevo, whereas previously you had confined yourself to Rajlovac. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked me about the tunnel. After the end of the war, after my meetings with a bunch of people from Sarajevo, I am hearing stories about how they went out through the tunnel. I'm talking about the tunnel, not about Sarajevo, that people were leaving Sarajevo through the tunnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, tanks --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. It was only right that you should be able to answer that comment from counsel. Yes, Mr. Waespi, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just the last point of that. Why, if you have any information to that extent, did the civilians inside Sarajevo not leave through the tunnel if they were free to do? Why did they stay inside the city, suffering, trapped inside the city? Do you have any comment, any explanation about that? If it was so easy to leave, why didn't they leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say why someone did not leave. I can give you my own example. My mother-in-law - I don't know how you will interpret that - left Sarajevo in 1994. She probably could have left earlier. People were coming in and people were going out. And I can say how many people were brought to us to Ilidza via UNPROFOR from Sarajevo and went out through Kiseljak. And then probably they returned again. There was some police reports referring to these things, and it was said that this was something that was done quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now move on a couple of weeks further in the period you describe as a lull. Are you aware that in December of 1994, UNPROFOR assessed the situation that the Serbs made it almost impossible to have pushed UNPROFOR to the brink of withdrawal; for instance, by not allowing any humanitarian convoys into the city, again almost no gas in the city, and the Serbs firing small guided missiles and anti-tank rockets into the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Waespi, I'm sorry. The explanation that the witness gave is not in the transcript at all, but when I allowed him to offer an explanation in relation to the question you asked as to why he was now able to speak about Sarajevo. So I hope it will be put in the transcript when the transcript is corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to my next point, the next set of facts relating to the period that you described as a lull, is an assessment by UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Contained, Mr. President, Your Honours, in Exhibit P10, Prosecution Exhibit 10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- Where it says the Serbs made the UNPROFOR task almost impossible: "Having pushed UNPROFOR to the brink of withdrawal by not allowing any humanitarian convoys into the city, again almost no gas in the city, and the Serbs firing small guided missiles and anti-tank rockets into the down-town area causing a number of civilian casualties." That's on page 1 and 6 of Prosecution Exhibit 10. Is that something you would also have information about, you're an intelligence officer, you were stationed in Rajlovac, occasionally in Butmir, was that also the assessment you made about the situation in December 1994, a couple of months into the tenure of the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After the witness answers, we'll take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that UNPROFOR did not really move around a lot through Rajlovac. UNPROFOR mostly moved through Kiseljak, Blazuj, Ilidza, and Sarajevo. Those were the routes they used. UNPROFOR would go, there would be humanitarian aid, I cannot recall the date when either the military or civilian police stopped a convoy and found some bullet-proof jackets. We received information that there was some weapons there. Also I don't know if that was the reason, I do not remember, but I remember that that caused tension in relations between the VRS and UNPROFOR. And I know through information we received later whether the bullet-proof vests were returned or not. Perhaps they were kept at Ilidza. I don't know if it was intended for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to UNPROFOR. I don't know about that, but it does say there that it was stopped at Ilidza. There was also a convoy of humanitarian aid that was moving from Kiseljak towards Sarajevo. I know that things like that did happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. On that note we'll take the adjournment until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
